steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write a short introduction for our paper on measuring moral inconsistency in LLMs. Motivate why consistency on moral questions matters and why existing uncertainty measures fall short, then introduce our Semantic Graph Entropy metric and summarise the approach and findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:

2. Limits of existing uncertainty / consistency measures
3. Our metric: Semantic Graph Entropy (SGE)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Building powerful Large Language Models (LLMs) that solve complicated tasks is important, but making sure they are reliable is just as critical. If an LLM can make consistent decisions in contexts that are semantically equivalent, it is considered more reliable and trustworthy. This is a commonplace problem when users talk to LLMs about moral queries, since it can impact the users a lot. Recent works have also shown that even popular LLMs like ChatGPT can be inconsistent. So it is essential to assess the consistency of a model before it is deployed in the real world.

Related work measures uncertainty at the word/token level, and on tasks that have a ground truth. In moral or superhuman scenarios this is harder to do because there is no correct answer.

We propose Semantic Graph Entropy (SGE), which is an information-theoretic metric for measuring consistency in LLMs. SGE uses the uncertainty estimation that entropy gives and combines it with semantic embedding methods so that it gives a reliable measure of consistency. We show empirically that SGE is a better metric for assessing consistency by comparing it to previously proposed metrics.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Building powerful Large Language Models (LLMs) that solve complicated tasks is important, but making sure they are reliable is just as critical. If an LLM can make consistent decisions in contexts that are semantically equivalent, it is considered more reliable and trustworthy. This is a commonplace problem when users talk to LLMs about moral queries, since it can impact the users a lot. Recent works have also shown that even popular LLMs like ChatGPT can be inconsistent. So it is essential to assess the consistency of a model before it is deployed in the real world.

Related work measures uncertainty at the word/token level, and on tasks that have a ground truth. In moral or superhuman scenarios this is harder to do because there is no correct answer.

We propose Semantic Graph Entropy (SGE), which is an information-theoretic metric for measuring consistency in LLMs. SGE uses the uncertainty estimation that entropy gives and combines it with semantic embedding methods so that it gives a reliable measure of consistency. We show empirically that SGE is a better metric for assessing consistency by comparing it to previously proposed metrics.

Our approach has three parts, shown in Figure 1. First, we generate high-quality paraphrases for 10,000 queries in the Moral Integrity Corpus (MIC). Second, we use five LLMs to generate answers to these queries, and we generate Rules of Thumb (RoTs), which explain the decision-making strategies of a model when it generates responses. Third, we examine LLM consistency quantitatively with four metrics and we also do human evaluations. Our experiments show that the mainstream LLMs are inconsistent, and this emphasizes the issue of moral uncertainty in LLMs. Our approach is unsupervised, it works for BlackBox LLMs, and it quantifies the consistency of LLMs reliably.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Although building powerful Large Language Models (LLMs) to solve complicated tasks is important, ensuring that they are reliable is equally critical. An LLM that makes consistent decisions in semantically equivalent contexts is considered more reliable and trustworthy ([1], [2]). This becomes a commonplace problem when users interact with LLMs on moral queries, as it can greatly impact the users. Further, recent works have shown that even popular LLMs like ChatGPT can be inconsistent [3]. Therefore, assessing a model's consistency before deploying it in the real world is essential [4]. Related work measures uncertainty at a word/token level, and on tasks with ground truth ([5], [1]). This is harder to achieve in moral or superhuman scenarios, where there is no correct answer [6].

We propose Semantic Graph Entropy (SGE), an information-theoretic metric to measure consistency in LLMs. SGE harnesses the uncertainty estimation provided by entropy and pairs it with semantic embedding methods to provide a reliable measure of consistency. We empirically show that SGE is a better metric for assessing consistency by comparing it with previously proposed metrics ([2], [7]). Figure 1 illustrates our three-fold approach. First, we generate high-quality paraphrases for 10,000 queries in the Moral Integrity Corpus (MIC) [8]. Second, we use five LLMs to generate answers to these queries and generate Rules of Thumb (RoTs), which explain a model's decision-making strategies while generating responses [9]. Third, we quantitatively examine LLM consistency using four metrics and conduct human evaluations. Our experiments show that mainstream LLMs are inconsistent, emphasizing the issue of moral uncertainty in LLMs. Our approach is unsupervised, works for BlackBox LLMs, and reliably quantifies LLM consistency.
